messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Product Manager
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo Reyes is a 22-year-old Colombian American product manager who presented for treatment following a period of escalating distress that had begun to interfere meaningfully with his professional functioning and daily life. He had grown up between Bogotá and Miami, and at nineteen had returned to Colombia for an extended visit with extended family in a region that, during his stay, became the site of sustained armed conflict between paramilitary factions and government forces. Over the course of three weeks, Mateo witnessed street-level violence, was present during a firefight that passed through his relatives' neighborhood, and spent nearly two days sheltering in a basement while gunfire and explosions sounded at irregular intervals above him. The uncertainty of that confinement — never knowing whether the next sound meant the fighting was approaching or receding, whether a shadow moving past the basement window was a soldier or something worse — left a particular imprint. It was the unpredictability of movement and sound, more than any single moment, that had saturated those days with terror.

He returned to the United States several months later and enrolled in college, completing his degree and moving into a junior product manager role at a mid-sized tech firm in Miami. For a time, the pace of work and the structure of his new professional life seemed to contain things. But over the following two years, a persistent and exhausting alertness settled into his body that he could not will away. Mateo described his physical state as one of constant readiness — muscles held tight across his shoulders and jaw, a baseline tension he noticed most acutely in meetings or open-plan office spaces where colleagues moved freely around him. When someone walked quickly into his peripheral vision or a coworker appeared suddenly at his desk, his body reacted before his mind could intervene — a sharp flinch, a surge of alarm, a momentary certainty that something was coming. In the open-plan environment where he spent most of his working hours, this happened multiple times a day.

He had developed the habit of scanning his own body throughout the day, checking his hands for steadiness, monitoring his heartbeat, pressing fingers against his forearm to assess whether the tension he felt was normal or a sign that something was genuinely wrong. What frightened him most, he explained, was the possibility that his body was registering a real threat that his conscious mind had failed to identify — that the alarm was informative rather than mistaken. This belief made the checking feel not compulsive but rational, even necessary.

In the months after symptoms intensified, Mateo began reaching out to friends and his older sister with increasing frequency, asking whether he seemed okay, whether they thought he was handling things normally, whether they were worried about him. He was aware that these conversations had become repetitive, and he had noticed his sister's responses growing briefer, her reassurances delivered with a flatness that told him she was tired of the question. Two close friendships had grown strained in ways he attributed to his own neediness, and he found himself cycling between relief after reassurance and renewed doubt within hours.

On several occasions over the past four months, during moments of acute overwhelm — typically following a particularly jarring startle response at work or a night of disrupted sleep — Mateo had hurt himself physically, pressing his nails hard into his skin or striking his thigh, describing it as the only thing that cut through a feeling he could not otherwise locate or discharge. He had told no one about this.

What finally brought him to seek help was a performance review in which his manager noted that he seemed distracted and reactive in collaborative settings, and asked whether everything was all right. Mateo had said yes, then gone home and sat for a long time trying to understand how visible he had become. He arrived at the intake appointment hoping, above all, that someone could explain to him why his body had not yet understood that he was safe — and quietly terrified that the answer might be that it was right not to.
